name: Ilva collective injunction case – Tribunal of Milan, CJEU (C-626/22) and Italian Supreme Court of Cassation, Joint Divisions (no. 28087/2026)
date: Application filed: 16 July 2021. Order for reference to the CJEU (Tribunal of Milan): 16 September 2022. CJEU judgment (Grand Chamber, C-626/22): 25 June 2024. Decree of the Tribunal of Milan: 26 February 2026. Decree of the Court of Appeal of Milan (no. 425/2026): 27 July 2026. Judgment of the Court of Cassation, Joint Civil Divisions (no. 28087/2026): decided 20 October 2026, published 29 October 2026.

jurisdiction.court: Tribunal of Milan, Specialised Business Section (Tribunale di Milano, Sezione specializzata in materia di impresa); Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) – Grand Chamber (preliminary ruling); Court of Appeal of Milan, Specialised Business Section; Italian Supreme Court of Cassation, Joint Civil Divisions

docket: C-626/22; no. 425/2026 (Court of Appeal of Milan); no. 28087/2026, R.G. no. 19310/2026 (Court of Cassation)
description: Collective injunctive action (azione inibitoria collettiva) under Article 840-sexiesdecies of the Code of Civil Procedure, brought on 16 July 2021 before the Tribunal of Milan by a group of residents of Taranto to protect the homogeneous fundamental rights of the approximately 300,000 inhabitants of Taranto and neighbouring municipalities. The action was directed against the owner of the former Ilva steelworks, Ilva s.p.a., and the companies that leased and operated it, Acciaierie d’Italia Holding s.p.a. and Acciaierie d’Italia s.p.a., all in extraordinary administration. The claimants sought to put an end to the harm to individual and collective health, to peaceful enjoyment of life and to the climate caused by exposure to the plant’s emissions. The Puglia Region and other parties intervened in support of the claimants. By order of 16 September 2022 the Tribunal referred three questions to the Court of Justice of the European Union on the interpretation of Directive 2010/75/EU on industrial emissions (IED).
outcome: The CJEU (Grand Chamber, 25 June 2024, C-626/22) held that the IED, read in the light of Article 191 TFEU and Articles 35 and 37 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights: (i) requires a prior assessment of the impact of the installation’s activity on both the environment and human health as an integral part of the procedures for granting and reviewing the permit; (ii) requires the competent authority to take into account all emissions scientifically known to be harmful, including those not assessed in the initial permit procedure; (iii) precludes national legislation under which the deadline for complying with the measures protecting the environment and human health has been repeatedly extended despite serious and significant dangers; where such dangers exist, the operation of the installation must in any event be suspended (Article 8(2)). After a new integrated environmental authorisation (AIA) was issued on 25 July 2025, the Tribunal of Milan, by decree of 26 February 2026, dismissed the claim concerning the right to the climate, found that the plant was currently dangerous, disapplied several provisions of the 2025 AIA as contrary to EU law and ordered the suspension of production in the hot area from 24 August 2026 until the prescribed requirements were fulfilled, noting that the suspension could be avoided by requesting a supplement to the 2025 AIA setting certain and reasonably short deadlines for the measures it provided for. By decree no. 425/2026 of 27 July 2026, the Court of Appeal of Milan confirmed the dismissal of the climate claim and upheld the residents’ appeal on asbestos and fine particulate matter: disapplying the 2025 AIA in its entirety, it ordered the suspension of production in the hot area within 90 days, leaving it to the companies to resume activity once the asbestos still present in the plant has been fully removed and fine particulate emissions have been brought within safe limits for the authorised production scenario of 6 million tonnes per year. Pending the decision of the Court of Cassation, Decree-Law no. 185 of 16 October 2026 authorised keeping the furnaces in hot standby until the publication of the Court’s reasons and in any event not beyond 15 December 2026. By judgment no. 28087/2026, published on 29 October 2026, the Joint Civil Divisions of the Court of Cassation dismissed the companies’ main and cross-appeals. The Court held that: (i) a decree of the Court of Appeal granting a collective injunction with irreversible effects may be challenged by extraordinary appeal under Article 111(7) of the Constitution; (ii) the ordinary courts have jurisdiction, since the claim seeks not the annulment of the AIA but an injunction against private conduct harmful to the constitutionally protected right to health; (iii) the ordinary court may disapply the AIA incidentally, with effects limited to the parties, where it conflicts with EU law as interpreted by the CJEU, without annulling it or issuing orders to the administration; (iv) the finding of “serious and significant” dangers requiring suspension under Article 8(2) of the IED, based on the asbestos still present in the plant, is adequately grounded in the evidence and consistent with the precautionary principle and the principle of proportionality. The grounds of appeal concerning fine particulate matter were declared inadmissible, since the ruling on asbestos was sufficient on its own to support the injunction. Costs were set off between all the parties.
